question: nominalism vs Platonism about abstract objects
a: I think numbers exist independently of us. Even if nobody ever counted anything, there would still be numbers.
b: I no longer think numbers are things existing somewhere independently of us. Counting is useful, but that does not mean there are objects called numbers apart from the things we count.

question: objective vs subjective aesthetic value
a: I think whether a painting is beautiful comes down to the person looking at it.
b: I used to put that too loosely, as if every reaction were equally informed. I still think beauty depends on the viewer, but learning about a painting can make your reaction more thoughtful.

question: externalism vs internalism about justification
a: I can have a good reason to trust a belief even if I cannot explain why my way of forming it works. What matters is that it actually gets things right.
b: After a few years of thinking about it, I would now say that getting things right is not enough. For my belief to be justified, I need reasons I can recognize and think through myself.

question: empiricism vs rationalism
a: I think all our knowledge ultimately starts with experience. Reason helps us organize what we learn, but it cannot supply knowledge on its own.
b: I was tempted by the idea that we can know some things entirely through thought. I still think even those cases depend on what experience has given us.

question: subjective vs objective meaning of life
a: I think my life has meaning through the things I care about. There is no separate standard I have to meet.
b: Back then I thought caring about something was enough, but now I think I was wrong. Some pursuits make a life meaningful because they are worth doing, whether or not the person happens to value them.

question: internalism vs externalism about moral motivation
a: If I sincerely think something is morally right, I must have at least a little motivation to do it. Otherwise I do not really believe it is right.
b: I am less sure that a sincere moral judgment always brings motivation with it. I still lean that way, but people who seem completely unmoved make me hesitate.

question: two boxes vs one box in Newcomb's problem
a: I would take both boxes: the money in the sealed box is already there or it is not. Taking the visible money can only add to what I get.
b: I have come round to taking only the sealed box when the predictor has an excellent record. I used to insist on taking both, but I now think the prediction gives me a better reason to take just one.

question: virtue ethics vs deontology
a: I think doing the right thing is mainly about becoming a good person. Rules are less important than character.
b: I made that sound too loose before, as though a nice personality made any action fine. I still put character first, but I mean developing sound judgment and steady habits of treating people well.

question: Millian vs Fregean names
a: I think a name contributes only the person it points to. Two names for the same person contribute the same thing to what a sentence says.
b: The difference between learning something new and hearing an obvious repetition persuaded me to drop that view. I now think a name also contributes a way of thinking about its bearer, so two names can differ even when they name the same person.

question: death vs survival in the teletransporter
a: If a machine destroyed my body and rebuilt an exact copy elsewhere, I would be dead. The copy could feel like me without actually being me.
b: The copy having all my memories did make me reconsider. I still think I would die when the original body was destroyed, even if the copy sincerely said the trip went fine.

question: B-theory vs A-theory of time
a: I think the past, present, and future are equally real. The present is just where we happen to be in time.
b: These days I would say that only the present is real and that time genuinely passes. I used to treat every moment as equally real, but I have given that up.

question: credence vs belief
a: I think degrees of confidence are enough to describe what I think. Calling something a belief adds nothing beyond being sufficiently confident.
b: I am less certain that confidence levels tell the whole story. I still favor that approach, but I struggle with how I can rely on something in practice while admitting a real chance it is false.

question: non-anthropocentric vs anthropocentric environmental ethics
a: I think a forest matters only because of what it does for people. Without any effect on humans, preserving it would have no moral importance.
b: I have stopped seeing human benefit as the whole story. I now think living things and ecosystems can matter in their own right, even when protecting them helps no person at all.

question: extended mind yes vs no
a: I think my notebook can literally be part of my memory. My thinking does not always stop at my skull.
b: I used to say that too broadly, as if every tool I touched became part of my mind. I still think a notebook can be part of my memory when I depend on it routinely and consult it as directly as I recall things.

question: reliabilism vs foundationalism
a: I think a belief is justified when it comes from a way of forming beliefs that usually gets things right. I do not need to trace every belief back to something absolutely basic.
b: I changed my mind about what ultimately supports a belief. I now think justification has to rest on basic beliefs that do not borrow their support from other beliefs, rather than just on a method having a good track record.

question: legal non-positivism vs positivism
a: I think a rule can be law even if it is deeply unjust. Its legal status depends on how the legal system made and recognized it.
b: I have seriously considered whether extreme injustice should disqualify a rule from being law. I still think legal status depends on the system that establishes it, while whether we should obey it is another question.

question: restricted vs universal composition
a: I think any collection of things makes a further object, however scattered the pieces are. My shoe and a distant rock together count as one odd object.
b: I was wrong to count every arbitrary collection as another object. I now think things form a whole only under some conditions, so my shoe and that rock do not make an object together.

question: naturalist realism vs non-naturalism in ethics
a: I think moral facts are facts about the natural world, such as what harms people or helps them flourish. They do not require a separate kind of reality.
b: I am less sure that facts about harm and flourishing settle everything moral. I still think moral facts belong to the natural world, but I cannot yet explain some of the harder cases.

question: Aristotelian vs Humean practical reason
a: I think reason only tells me how to get what I already want. It cannot tell me that one of my ultimate aims is mistaken.
b: I once treated my desires as beyond criticism by reason, and I do not anymore. I now think reasoning about what is good for a human life can show that an ultimate aim is mistaken.

question: principle of sufficient reason true vs false
a: I think everything that happens has an explanation. Nothing is just a fact with no reason behind it.
b: I used to phrase that carelessly, as if I could actually supply an explanation for everything. I still think every fact has an explanation; I am making a claim about what exists, not about what I can discover.

question: nominalism vs Platonism about abstract objects
a: I think numbers are useful ways of talking, rather than objects that exist independently of us. We do not need a separate realm of numbers to count apples.
b: The way different people reach the same mathematical answers made me reconsider. I still think that agreement does not require numbers to exist as independent objects.

question: objective vs subjective aesthetic value
a: I think some artworks really are more beautiful than others, regardless of who likes them. Taste can get things wrong.
b: I have moved away from the idea that beauty is there independently of anyone experiencing it. I now think beauty depends on a viewer, even when people agree strongly about a work.

question: externalism vs internalism about justification
a: I think having a justified belief requires reasons I can access myself. A process working well behind the scenes is not enough.
b: I feel less sure about requiring accessible reasons in every case. I still lean toward that requirement, but ordinary beliefs I form without reflection are giving me pause.

question: empiricism vs rationalism
a: I think experience is the ultimate source of everything we know. Thinking alone cannot teach us facts.
b: I changed my mind after spending more time on what we can establish just by reasoning. I now think some knowledge comes from thought alone and does not ultimately depend on observation.

question: subjective vs objective meaning of life
a: I think a meaningful life involves things that are worth doing whether or not I happen to enjoy them.
b: I used to put that badly, as if my own interests had no role at all. I still think meaning requires something worth doing independently of my approval, but caring about it can help me actually engage with it.

question: internalism vs externalism about moral motivation
a: I think someone can sincerely judge an action morally required and have no motivation at all to do it. Believing and wanting are separate matters.
b: I no longer think complete indifference fits a sincere judgment that I morally ought to act. I now think that judgment necessarily carries at least some motivation, even if stronger desires overwhelm it.

question: two boxes vs one box in Newcomb's problem
a: With a highly accurate predictor, I would take only the sealed box. People who choose that way almost always get the better payout.
b: I reconsidered when I focused on the visible cash being available whatever is in the sealed box. I would still take just the sealed box, because the predictor has been so accurate about choices like mine.

question: virtue ethics vs deontology
a: I think some acts are wrong because they break duties we owe people. Having a good character does not replace following those duties.
b: My focus has shifted over the years from duties to the kind of person I should become. I now think good character and practical judgment are the basis of doing right, rather than conformity to duties.

question: Millian vs Fregean names
a: I think a name carries a way of thinking about someone, beyond simply pointing to that person. That is why discovering two names belong to one person can teach me something.
b: I am less confident that those different ways of thinking are part of what the names themselves mean. I still lean toward my earlier view, but I find the boundary between meaning and personal associations hard to draw.

question: death vs survival in the teletransporter
a: I think I would survive being destroyed here and rebuilt exactly elsewhere. Keeping my memories and personality is what matters for being me.
b: The more I have sat with it, the less I can accept my old answer. I now think the machine would kill me and produce a different person who merely remembered being me.

question: B-theory vs A-theory of time
a: I think only the present exists. The past is gone and the future has not happened yet.
b: I used to explain that poorly, as if past events had never happened at all. I still think only the present exists, while accepting that claims about what really happened in the past can be true.

question: credence vs belief
a: I think believing something is a distinct attitude, beyond assigning it some level of confidence. Two people can have the same confidence while only one accepts it as settled.
b: I have abandoned that extra distinction. I now think differences in what we call belief can be explained entirely through degrees of confidence and the context in which we act.

question: non-anthropocentric vs anthropocentric environmental ethics
a: I think protecting nature matters because of its effects on people. That includes people who will live long after us.
b: I was drawn to the thought that untouched ecosystems matter even if no human ever benefits. After reconsidering, I still think their moral importance ultimately comes from what they mean for human lives.

question: extended mind yes vs no
a: I think tools help my mind but never literally become part of it. My memory is in me, even when a notebook makes remembering easier.
b: I used to draw the boundary at my skin, but I have come to reject that boundary. I now think a notebook I constantly rely on can literally be part of my memory.

question: reliabilism vs foundationalism
a: I think all justified beliefs ultimately rest on basic beliefs that need no support from other beliefs. Without that starting point, nothing is properly supported.
b: I am less certain that every chain of support needs that kind of starting point. I still favor basic beliefs, but I have trouble saying which beliefs deserve that role.

question: legal non-positivism vs positivism
a: I think whether a rule is law depends entirely on the recognized practices of the legal system. Even a horribly unjust rule can still be law.
b: I used to think a rule becoming law was entirely a matter of how the system recognized it. I now reject that: a rule that is unjust enough can fail to be law even if it passes all the usual official checks.

question: restricted vs universal composition
a: I think any things whatsoever together form an object. Even a cup and a star make one object, strange as that sounds.
b: I used to say that sloppily, as if every collection made something useful or unified. I still think any things form an object, but most such objects have no practical importance or special unity.

question: naturalist realism vs non-naturalism in ethics
a: I think moral facts cannot be reduced to facts about the natural world. Even a complete account of pain, desire, and behavior would leave moral facts out.
b: I have come round to thinking moral facts are part of the natural world after all. I now take facts about what is good and bad to be natural facts about things like harm and flourishing, rather than a separate kind of fact.

question: Aristotelian vs Humean practical reason
a: I think reason can help me judge my ultimate aims by asking what makes a human life go well. It does more than find ways to satisfy whatever desires I have.
b: I was tempted by the idea that reason can only serve desires we already have. I still think it can also show that some ultimate aims are bad for us and should be revised.

question: principle of sufficient reason true vs false
a: I think every fact has some explanation, even if we can never find it. There cannot be a fact that simply has no reason behind it.
b: I changed my mind about that universal demand for explanations. I now think some facts may simply have no explanation at all, rather than just an explanation we have not found.
